young.html: Where do your ideas come from? Were you born knowing what red is, or what a lemon tastes like? John Locke said no. He said a baby's mind is like a sheet of blank white paper, and experience writes on it.
Experience comes in two ways. Sensation is what your senses bring in: colors, sounds, tastes, hot and cold. Reflection is noticing what your own mind does: thinking, remembering, wanting, doubting.
Locke said simple ideas are like building blocks. Your mind puts them together to make bigger ideas. "Apple" is red + round + sweet + crunchy + a certain smell, all joined together.

young.name: gb-idea-builder
young.cap: Pick simple ideas and watch the mind join them into a complex idea.

young.html: Mystery bag. Put a few things in a bag (a spoon, an orange, a feather). Without looking, one person feels an object and names only simple ideas: "cold, smooth, hard, curved." Can the others guess it? Then talk: could you know what an orange is if you had never seen, smelled, touched or tasted one?

full.text: A book that began with a puzzle

full.html: Locke tells us the Essay (1689) began when friends meeting in his room got stuck on a hard question. He suggested they should first find out what the human mind is fit to know. Nearly twenty years later the answer filled four books.

Many thinkers held that some ideas and principles are stamped on the mind at birth, such as "whatever is, is" or the idea of God. Locke argues against this. If such ideas were innate, children and every people on earth would know them, and they plainly don't. Better, he says, to see how the mind gets its ideas.

full.text: Book II: all ideas from experience

Let us then suppose the mind to be, as we say, white paper, void of all characters, without any ideas; how comes it to be furnished? Whence comes it by that vast store which the busy and boundless fancy of man has painted on it, with an almost endless variety? Whence has it all the materials of reason and knowledge? To this I answer, in one word, from experience: in that all our knowledge is founded, and from that it ultimately derives itself.
full.author: John Locke
full.ed: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Thomas Tegg, London

full.html: The two "fountains" are sensation and reflection. From them come simple ideas, which the mind can't make up itself, and from those the mind builds complex ideas by combining, comparing and abstracting: ideas of substances (gold, a horse), of modes (a dozen, beauty, a lie) and of relations (father, bigger, cause).

full.name: gb-idea-builder
full.cap: Choose a thing, then switch its simple ideas on and off. Which ones come from sensation, and which from reflection?

full.html: Locke draws a famous line. Primary qualities, such as solidity, size, shape, motion and number, are really in objects, and our ideas of them resemble them. Secondary qualities, such as colors, sounds, tastes, smells and warmth, are powers in objects to produce ideas in us. There is no "sweetness" in sugar the way there is shape in it. Locke uses a simple test: the same water can feel warm to one hand and cold to the other.

head: Primary (in the thing)
Secondary (powers to cause ideas in us)

full.text: Persons, words and the limits of knowledge

full.html: In a famous chapter Locke asks what makes you the same person over time. Not the same body or even the same soul-stuff, he says, but the same consciousness: what you can remember as your own. Book III warns that many quarrels come from words used without clear ideas. Book IV says knowledge is the perception that ideas agree or disagree, and that it is narrower than we hope. Where we lack knowledge, we must live by probability and judgment, holding beliefs with the strength the evidence gives.
Thinking Locke said the mind is passive. The "white paper" receives simple ideas, but the mind is busy: it compares, combines, abstracts and reflects on its own operations.

deep.html: The Essay made Locke the leader of what later historians call British empiricism, the view that knowledge comes from experience. George Berkeley and David Hume, the next two rungs, start from Locke and push his ideas further. Berkeley asked why primary qualities should be any different from secondary ones. Hume asked where our idea of cause comes from. Kant, later in this era, tried to show that experience alone can't explain how we know some things for certain.

Locke's account of personal identity is still discussed by philosophers, as are his ideas on education (in Some Thoughts Concerning Education, 1693), which shaped how many families taught their children.

Leibniz wrote a long reply, New Essays on Human Understanding, arguing that the mind is more like a block of marble with veins in it: it has tendencies that experience brings out. Modern research on infants finds that babies come ready to learn some things quickly, such as faces and language sounds, which many take as a partial answer to Locke, though the debate about what is inborn continues.
